item.description: Far from pocket change, these large silver coins helped fund the defense of kingdoms Thalers are silver coins minted in the Holy Roman Empire and Prussia from the 16th to 19th centuries. item.title: Tales From the Vault: The Joy of Jetons - American Numismatic Association
item.description: King Louis XV struck tokens to popularize France’s American colonies and encourage emigration. item.title: Tales From the Vault - The Markoff Collection - American Numismatic Association
item.description: In 1979, the Money Museum received an incredible donation combining numismatic and presidential history. The Elliott Markoff Collection consists of 38 custom-made Capital Plastics holders featuring every U.S. President from George Washington to Jimmy Carter.

item.title: Tales From the Vault - Swedish Plate Money: Too Heavy to Steal! - American Numismatic Association
item.description: Sweden's large copper lumps or “plates” ranged in weight from 378g (just under a pound) to a staggering 23.8kg (more than 53 pounds!), the largest coins ever minted at the time. Hammered into sheets of the necessary thickness, they were then cut to size with shears and stamped. Four corner stamps bore the ruler’s name or initials along with the year of issue, while the center one denoted denomination. The reverse is blank. The pieces themselves are works of art. item.title: Tales From the Vault - Golden California: The Era of Private Coinage - American Numismatic Association
item.description: This remarkable collection, generously donated by Dr. Carlson Chambliss, captures a glittering panorama of California’s private gold coinage – including pieces from nearly every issuing firm. Together, they tell a story of necessity: the need to relieve a desperate shortage of trusted money in a land awash with raw gold. Their role, however, was temporary.
